summaries.example: Imagine a line of school events: a play rehearsal, a concert, and a sports day. We usually say one happened earlier and another later. McTaggart argued that this order may be real while the changing labels “future,” “present,” and “past” create a problem. He thought reality might be timeless, even though our experiences seem to happen in time.
summaries.summary: John McTaggart was a philosopher who studied the deepest questions about reality. He wrote about Hegel, time, minds, religion, parts and wholes, and ethics. His most famous argument says that time cannot be fully real because events would need to be future, present, and past, but these descriptions conflict. He therefore thought that time is an appearance built on a deeper, timeless order. McTaggart also argued that reality consists of many immaterial selves and their mental states. These selves are connected by relations such as perception and love. He rejected belief in a personal God, yet described his own view as mystical because he believed the universe had a profound unity. In ethics, he treated goodness and badness as real qualities and gave love a very important place.
key_ideas: McTaggart carefully studied big questions about reality and tried to make arguments clear.
He argued that time is not truly real, although our experiences and statements about earlier and later may still reflect a deeper order.
He thought reality is made of immaterial persons, or spirits, who can perceive and love one another.
He was an atheist but also called himself a mystic because he believed the universe had a deep unity connected with love.
He believed love is one of the greatest kinds of goodness.
summaries.why_it_matters: McTaggart shows how one philosophical idea can connect many subjects. Asking whether time is real leads to questions about change, perception, minds, religion, and value. His work also teaches an important habit: separate what seems obvious from what can be supported by an argument. Even when people reject his conclusions, they can study how he defined terms, compared possibilities, and tried to reason carefully.

important_terms.definition: The study of what reality is like at the deepest level, including questions about time, minds, and what exists.
The idea that reality is made up of minds or persons and their experiences, rather than physical matter alone.
The view that there are many basic selves or beings, not just one single thing.
A connection between things, such as one person noticing or caring about another.

questions_to_think_about: If clocks and calendars help us organize life, would time still seem unreal to you?
Can people disagree about religion while still taking religious questions seriously?
What makes a group of people a group rather than one person?
Can something be valuable even if it sometimes causes difficulties?

summaries.example: Consider a timeline containing a past exam, today’s lesson, and tomorrow’s test. The B-series orders these events by earlier-than and later-than. The A-series adds the changing status of each event as future, present, or past. McTaggart argues that real change requires the A-series, because an event must move from future to present to past. But every event would need all three incompatible statuses. If the A-series is impossible, he concludes that time is unreal. He still allows that a non-temporal C-series may explain why some temporal judgments are better founded than others.
summaries.summary: John M. E. McTaggart developed a wide-ranging metaphysical system influenced by Hegel but eventually pursued through highly structured argument. He defined metaphysics as inquiry into ultimate reality and was skeptical that empirical science alone could settle such questions. His best-known argument distinguishes the B-series, in which events stand in earlier-than and later-than relations, from the A-series, in which events are future, present, or past. He maintained that real change requires the A-series, yet its incompatible determinations generate a contradiction. He therefore concluded that time is unreal. Nevertheless, he thought temporal appearances could correspond imperfectly to a deeper C-series. McTaggart’s idealism identifies reality with persons and their mental states, and his pluralism treats many selves and their relations as fundamental. He also defended strong claims about parts, necessary properties, existence, and value. His religious philosophy combined atheism with mysticism: he denied a personal God but held that reality is deeply unified through loving spirits. His ethics includes moral realism, a form of pluralism about value, criticism of vindictive punishment, and a special status for love.
key_ideas: McTaggart moved from an early Hegelian dialectical approach toward a more deductive style based largely on a priori reasoning.
He separated the B-series from the A-series and argued that the A-series produces contradiction, so time is unreal.
His denial of time was not a denial of every ordering: he proposed C-series structures that can explain why some temporal judgments are better grounded than others.
His ontological idealism holds that reality consists of selves and their states, while his realism about relations allows perception and other connections to be genuine.
He rejected both extreme monism and solipsism, defending a plurality of fundamental selves.
In ethics, he treated intrinsic value as real, regarded conscious beings or their states as its bearers, and gave love a central role.
summaries.why_it_matters: McTaggart is a useful case study in systematic philosophy. His conclusions about time, minds, and value are controversial, but they are connected by explicit definitions and arguments. Studying him helps readers see how views in metaphysics can affect philosophy of religion and ethics. It also highlights a continuing philosophical question: should ultimate reality be explained mainly through the world described by experience and science, or through abstract reasoning about what must be possible?

important_terms.definition: The systematic study of the ultimate nature of reality, pursued by examining basic concepts and arguments.
The ordering of events by relations such as earlier than and later than, without selecting a present moment.
The ordering of events as future, present, and past; McTaggart held that real time requires this ordering.
A proposed non-temporal ordering underlying the appearance of temporal order.
The view that what exists is ultimately composed of persons or selves and their mental states.
The view that more than one fundamental being exists and that relations between beings are real.
The view that a thing has some feature necessarily, so it could not exist without that feature.
The view that goodness and badness are genuine features that cannot be reduced entirely to nonmoral facts.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining change require a genuine present, or can change be understood through earlier and later relations alone?
If a theory conflicts with ordinary experience, what kind of argument would justify accepting it?
Could reality consist entirely of minds while our perceptions of physical objects are mistaken about their nature?
Should the total value of a world depend on the number of people in it as well as how well they live?
Is love valuable because of its effects, because of what it is, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose your class keeps a timeline of a science project. The planning meeting is earlier than the experiment, and the experiment is earlier than the report. That is one kind of order. Another kind labels each event future before it happens, present while it happens, and past afterward. McTaggart said the first order might remain in a deeper form, but the second creates a puzzle: every event would have to be future, present, and past. He concluded that time itself is unreal, even though some ways of arranging events are more accurate than others.
summaries.summary: John McTaggart was an early twentieth-century philosopher whose work joined metaphysics, philosophy of religion, idealism, pluralism, and ethics. He first worked extensively on Hegel, although he later abandoned the dialectical method he associated with Hegel. In his later method, he used definitions and a priori arguments to investigate reality. His famous argument about time separates the B-series, an order of earlier and later events, from the A-series, which describes events as future, present, and past. McTaggart argued that real change needs the A-series, but that every event would then receive incompatible descriptions. He concluded that time is unreal, while allowing that a C-series might explain the real order behind temporal appearances. His ontological idealism holds that reality consists of persons and their mental states. Unlike extreme monism, his view includes many selves and real relations between them. He was an atheist who nevertheless defended a mystical unity based on loving spirits. In ethics, he held that goodness is real, criticized revenge-based punishment, and argued that love has exceptional value.
key_ideas: McTaggart began as an interpreter of Hegel but later relied more on carefully organized, deductive arguments.
He argued that time is unreal because real change seems to require the A-series, whose descriptions of events conflict.
He did not think all order disappears when time is rejected; a C-series could preserve some real structure beneath temporal appearances.
His idealism says that the basic parts of reality are persons or immaterial selves, not material objects as we normally understand them.
He rejected the idea that reality is only one undivided thing and also rejected solipsism, the view that only one self exists.
His philosophy of religion combined atheism with mysticism, and his ethics treated love as an especially important good.
summaries.why_it_matters: McTaggart helps show why philosophical disputes are not always about isolated facts. His view of time affects his account of causation and immortality; his idealism affects his account of perception; and his view of reality supports his religious and ethical conclusions. His work also gives students practice in evaluating arguments that challenge everyday assumptions without simply dismissing ordinary experience.

important_terms.definition: The study of the most basic features of reality, such as what exists and whether time is real.
Reasoning that begins with general principles and draws conclusions from them rather than mainly collecting observations.
A kind of knowledge or claim that McTaggart thought could be reached through reasoning independent of particular experiences.
The order of events as earlier or later, without treating any moment as objectively present.
The order of events as future, present, and past.
A deeper, non-temporal ordering that McTaggart proposed might underlie our experience of time.
The belief that reality is made of persons or selves, including their mental states.
The belief that reality contains many fundamental beings and genuine connections among them.

questions_to_think_about: Are “earlier than” and “later than” enough to explain change, or must there be a real present?
Why might a philosopher think science cannot by itself answer questions about ultimate reality?
If our perceptions misrepresent the nature of objects, can they still tell us that something exists?
What is the difference between saying that many things are connected and saying that they are really one thing?
Should an ethical theory accept a result that seems troubling if its reasoning supports it?
